references.text: The Valley of Eshkol is mentioned again in connection with the spies' report and the people's discouragement after seeing the fertility of the land.
Moses recounts the story of the spies who came to the Valley of Eshkol and brought back fruit from the land as proof of its goodness.
Explains why the place was called the Valley of Eshkol, after the cluster of grapes (אֶשְׁכּוֹל) that the Israelites cut there.
Describes the promised land as a land of vineyards, fig trees, and pomegranate trees—the same fruits the spies brought back.
The first time Eshkol is mentioned in the Bible, as one of Abraham's allies, possibly connected to the area that later became known as the Valley of Eshkol.
The Song of Songs uses the image of a cluster of grapes from the vineyards of Engedi, reminiscent of the fertile cluster from Eshkol.
Isaiah's parable of the vineyard describes Israel as God's vineyard with choice vines, reflecting the land's fertility.
